To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

industry competition, as proxied by industry characteristics, has a significant positive relation with managerial incentives, and that the relation is stronger for smaller and less concentrated industries.
(a) the level of competition in an industry is positively related to managerial compensation and (b) this relation is multi-dimensional, reflecting the different aspects of industry competition.

(i) firms provide stronger incentive pay to their CEOs and CFOs when industry competition is stronger, (ii) competition is multi-dimensionally related to incentives, and (iii) industry characteristics play an important role in determining incentive pay.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relation between industry product market competition and the design and use of executive compensation contracts.
the role of industry competition and managerial incentives in the context of a firm's strategic decision-making process.
the role of industry product market competition on managerial incentives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
industry characteristics play an important role in determining the nature and strength of incentives.
industry competition can substitute for incentives, but this substitution is contingent upon the industry characteristics.
competition and incentives have a positive relation, but this relation depends on industry characteristics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the level of industry competition is positively associated with managerial incentives.
competition can be a substitute for or a complement to managerial incentives, and that this depends on the level of industry competition.

industry characteristics play an important role in the design of managerial incentives, and this is a result of the interaction of the industry characteristics with the firm’s characteristics, such as the firm’s size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between incentives and industry competition is more complex and nuanced than previously believed.
competition and incentives are related, but not in a uni-dimensional manner, and that industry characteristics matter in this relationship.
industry competition is a multi-dimensional construct that is not necessarily reflected in industry concentration.
